headline: Chicago is a city of sides with a Second City chip, and the Bulls play on Madison Street, the line where North and South Side addresses begin, which makes them the one team every side shares.
summary: Chicago sees itself the way Carl Sandburg wrote it in 1914: 'City of the Big Shoulders', a working city that rebuilt itself after the 1871 fire and took the nickname 'Second City', first meant as an East Coast jab, as a badge. It assumes the rest of the country knows it as flyover country or as a crime talking point, and it bristles at both. Identity runs through sides (North, South, West, the suburbs), 77 community areas, parishes and high schools, and a population that is roughly one-third Black, one-third Latino and one-third white, built by the Great Migration and generations of immigrants. Daily life is shaped by winter and the Hawk, and the city's calendar fills with parades from Bud Billiken to the green river. Nike's opening in a rebuild year is to make product that unites the sides, rooted in civic symbols locals actually use, built for January walks to the United Center and co-authored with the communities that make the city what it is.

insights.title: Second City, Big Shoulders
insights.detail: Chicagoans see themselves as blunt, hardworking and unpretentious: Sandburg's 'Hog Butcher for the World', Richard J. Daley's 'The City That Works', and the 'I Will' motto from the 1890s, when the city rose from the Great Fire to win the 1893 World's Fair. A.J. Liebling's 1952 New Yorker put-down 'The Second City' became a comedy institution and a point of pride, and locals know 'Windy City' is usually explained as a dig at its boastful promoters, not its weather.
insights.implication: Write the product voice in a working-class, understated register: earned, durable and a little defiant, not flashy. Public-domain civic language like 'City of the Big Shoulders' and 'I Will' fits a rebuild built on size and physicality better than another '90s victory lap.

insights.title: Madison Street runs through the arena
insights.detail: The street grid starts at State and Madison: everything north of Madison is a North address and everything south is a South address, and the United Center sits at 1901 W. Madison on the Near West Side, across the street from where Chicago Stadium stood. Baseball splits the city (Cubs North Side, Sox South Side), but the Bulls draw from every side and the suburbs, and locals still size each other up by side, neighborhood and 'Where'd you go to high school?'
insights.implication: Treat the Bulls as Chicago's unifier. Build North/South/West/suburbs product that adds up to one city rather than pitting sides against each other, and use grid coordinates, community areas and high-school pride as hyperlocal hooks.

insights.title: A Black-founded, Great Migration city
insights.detail: Chicago's first non-Native settler, Jean Baptiste Point DuSable, was a Black trader widely described as Haitian-born; Lake Shore Drive was renamed for him in 2021. From about 1916 to 1970, Black Southerners, many from the Mississippi Delta, came north on the Illinois Central, encouraged by Robert S. Abbott's Chicago Defender, and built Bronzeville into the 'Black Metropolis' of Ida B. Wells, Gwendolyn Brooks, Harold Washington and Mamie Till-Mobley. Since 2000 many Black families have moved to the 708 south suburbs.
insights.implication: Black Chicago is the Bulls' cultural engine. Co-author heritage product with its institutions (DuSable Museum, Chicago Defender Charities, South Side designers), credit and pay them, and stock it in the south suburbs as well as downtown.

insights.title: La Villita, Pilsen and Paseo Boricua under pressure
insights.detail: Latino Chicagoans are about 30 percent of the city (2020 Census), mostly Mexican in Pilsen and Little Village and Puerto Rican in Humboldt Park, whose activism goes back to the 1966 Division Street uprising. In fall 2025 a federal immigration enforcement surge centered on these neighborhoods, and residents organized rapid-response networks, including whistles to warn neighbors.
insights.implication: Latino fans are a core Bulls market, but 2026-27 activations must be bilingual, community-led and physically safe: partner with local designers and institutions such as the National Museum of Puerto Rican Arts & Culture, and never collect data, film residents or borrow protest imagery.

insights.title: Chicago grows the stars other cities win with
insights.detail: Chicago-area hoopers keep winning titles elsewhere: Isiah Thomas (West Side) with Detroit, Kevin Garnett (Farragut) with Boston, Dwyane Wade (Richards HS) with Miami, Anthony Davis (Englewood) with the Lakers, and in June 2026 Jalen Brunson (Stevenson HS, Lincolnshire) as Finals MVP for the Knicks. Derrick Rose, the Englewood and Simeon kid who became the 2011 MVP for his hometown team, is still the city's model of a homegrown star, and Simeon's No. 25 for Ben Wilson, killed in 1984, is Public League scripture.
insights.implication: Tell Chicago-made basketball stories (the Public League, Simeon, the Catholic League, park leagues) as the city's own heritage, then hand that pride to the Splitter-era core of Giddey, Buzelis and Caleb Wilson. Partner with the schools and families instead of taking their numbers and names.

insights.title: The home season is Hawk season
insights.detail: The NBA season runs through the months when 'the Hawk', the wind off Lake Michigan, makes 20 degrees feel like zero; the January 2019 polar vortex hit about -23F. Fans reach the United Center by the No. 20 Madison bus or a long walk from the nearest L stops, so the real fan uniform is a long parka, a knit hat and a hoodie under it, and summer is lived outside on the 18-mile lakefront.
insights.implication: Make outerwear the hero of Chicago game-day product: wind-blocking stadium parkas, heavyweight fleece, cuffed knits and gloves, with reflective details for dark walks, timed to drop before the first freeze. Pivot to lakefront-weight tees and shorts for the spring and summer parade season.

insights.title: Dynasty pride, ownership fatigue
insights.detail: The six titles (1991-93, 1996-98) and their Grant Park rallies are the city's last great shared sports celebration, and June 13, 2027 marks 30 years since Steve Kerr's title-clinching shot on Jordan's pass. Local pride now coexists with a 31-51 season and long frustration with the Reinsdorf era, which surfaced in booing during the January 2024 Ring of Honor ceremony.
insights.implication: Use the '90s through Jordan Brand with restraint and pair every legacy piece with the new core, so heritage feels like a promise rather than a substitute. Fan-made language beats official 'loyalty' messaging, which can read as tone-deaf in a rebuild.

places.name: State and Madison
places.why: The zero point of the address grid, once billed as 'the World's Busiest Corner': Madison divides North from South and State divides East from West, so every Chicago address counts from here.

places.name: DuSable Black History Museum and Education Center
places.why: Founded in 1961 by artist-educator Margaret Burroughs, it is one of the oldest independent Black history museums in the U.S. and the natural co-author for Black heritage stories.

places.name: Pullman National Historical Park and A. Philip Randolph Pullman Porter Museum
places.why: The company town, the 1894 strike and the Pullman porters' union tell the labor and Black history behind 'The City That Works'.

places.name: Little Village Arch ('Bienvenidos a Little Village')
places.why: The gateway to 26th Street, the Mexican commercial corridor often cited (unverified) as the city's second-busiest shopping strip after Michigan Avenue.

places.name: National Museum of Puerto Rican Arts & Culture
places.why: Housed in the park's historic stables near Paseo Boricua, it anchors Puerto Rican Chicago's cultural memory.

places.name: American Indian Center of Chicago
places.why: Founded in 1953, it is one of the oldest urban Native centers in the country and the right first call before any Native-related story or land acknowledgment.

places.name: Chicago History Museum
places.why: The city's archive from the Great Fire to the Bulls dynasty, and a credible partner for heritage capsules and archival graphics.

places.name: Promontory Point
places.why: A limestone-stepped peninsula where South Siders swim and watch the skyline, and a neighborhood-defended symbol of public lakefront access.

places.name: Al's #1 Italian Beef
places.why: Open since 1938 and the best place to learn the beef vocabulary (dipped, hot, sweet) every Chicagoan speaks.

places.name: Superdawg Drive-In
places.why: A 1948 Milwaukee Avenue drive-in with Maurie and Flaurie, the giant hot dog figures on the roof; a Northwest Side landmark of the city's hot dog culture.

people.name: Michael Jordan
people.why: A North Carolinian whom Chicago adopted; his statue 'The Spirit' and the six titles are the city's global calling card, available to Nike through Jordan Brand.

people.name: Derrick Rose
people.role: Englewood native, Simeon alum, 2011 NBA MVP
people.why: The hometown kid who became the league's youngest MVP is the most loved local Bull and the model of the homegrown star Chicago wants back.

people.name: Dwyane Wade
people.role: Hall of Famer, South Side native
people.why: A Richards High School product who won three titles in Miami and came home to play for the Bulls in 2016-17, so he embodies both Chicago's hoops pipeline and its pull.

people.name: Stacey King
people.role: Bulls TV analyst and '90s Bulls champion
people.why: His calls ('Gimme the hot sauce!', 'Kaboom!') are part of how local fans talk about the team.

people.name: Benny the Bull
people.why: Older than the dynasty and loved across generations, he is a ready-made character for kids' and family product.

people.name: Lena Waithe
people.role: Writer and producer, South Side native
people.why: She created Showtime's 'The Chi', which showed South Side family life to a national audience on its own terms.

people.name: The Second City
people.role: Improv theater in Old Town, founded 1959
people.why: It turned the city's 'Second City' put-down into a world-famous institution, the clearest example of Chicago owning its chip.

people.name: Chicago Defender Charities
people.role: Organizer of the Bud Billiken Parade
people.why: It carries the Chicago Defender's Great Migration legacy into the largest African American parade in the country.

moments.name: Bud Billiken Parade and Picnic
moments.why: Founded in 1929 by the Chicago Defender, this back-to-school parade down King Drive to Washington Park is the South Side's biggest day of the year.

moments.name: Mexican Independence Day Parade on 26th Street
moments.why: Little Village and Pilsen fill with flags, banda and lowriders, the clearest public expression of Mexican Chicago pride.

moments.name: Chinatown Lunar New Year Parade
moments.timing: Early-to-mid February (Lunar New Year is Feb. 6, 2027, Year of the Goat)
moments.why: Chinatown's in-season parade on Wentworth Avenue is a February moment for Chicago's Chinese American community.

moments.name: Chicago's birthday
moments.why: The city was incorporated on March 4, 1837; the 190th birthday falls mid-season and gives a natural hook for civic-symbol product.

moments.name: St. Patrick's river dyeing, parade and South Side Irish Parade
moments.timing: Saturday before March 17 (expected March 13, 2027), Beverly's parade that Sunday
moments.why: Plumbers Local 130 has dyed the Chicago River green since 1962, and Bridgeport and Beverly carry the Irish South Side identity.

moments.name: Puerto Rican Fest and People's Parade
moments.why: Humboldt Park and Paseo Boricua's flag-filled week of pride.

moments.name: Chicago Pride Parade
moments.why: One of the largest Pride parades in the U.S., running through Lakeview and Northalsted.

moments.name: 30th anniversary of the 1997 title
moments.why: Thirty years since Kerr's shot clinched title No. 5 at the United Center, landing during the playoffs as a heritage beat.

vocabulary.meaning: What Chicagoans call sneakers. The city that made the Air Jordan 1 a phenomenon rarely says 'sneakers' or 'tennis shoes'.
South and West Side term for any guy, as in 'You trippin', Joe' or 'That's crazy, Joe'.
The brutal winter wind off the lake, as in 'The Hawk is out'.
Claiming a shoveled street parking spot with lawn chairs or old furniture after a snowfall; a civic argument every winter.
What locals still call Willis Tower, decades after the name change; using the new name marks you as an outsider.
Everything in Illinois outside Chicagoland, including towns that are geographically north or west.

vocabulary.term: Where'd you go to high school?
vocabulary.meaning: The classic Chicago icebreaker, which instantly places someone by side, neighborhood, parish and class.
The standard Italian beef order: the sandwich dunked in jus with spicy giardiniera ('sweet' means roasted peppers).

designCues.cue: Grid coordinates: '0 N/S, 0 E/W' for State and Madison paired with '1901 W. Madison', the United Center's address on the line that splits North from South.
designCues.source: Chicago's address grid, which counts every address from State and Madison at 800 numbers to the mile.
designCues.use: Neck tapes, sleeve hits and split-panel graphics that put North and South on one garment. It is ideal for a unity-themed City or fan collection.

designCues.cue: The municipal 'Y' device: a three-pronged Y standing for the Chicago River's main stem and its North and South branches.
designCues.source: The city symbol cast on bridges, park buildings and older municipal structures.
designCues.use: A small hidden mark (jock tag, waistband, knit-cuff patch) that locals will spot. Confirm the City's usage rules first.

designCues.cue: 'I Will' and 'City of the Big Shoulders' set in heavy condensed industrial capitals, like stencils on rail cars and grain elevators.
designCues.source: The 1890s civic motto and Carl Sandburg's 1914 poem 'Chicago' (public domain).
designCues.use: Interior prints and shooting-shirt backs for the rebuild, giving the new size-and-physicality identity a civic voice.

designCues.cue: Area-code numerals 312, 773, 708, 630 and 847, set in Bulls-style block numbers.
designCues.source: 312 was the city's original code, 773 has covered the neighborhoods since 1996, and 708, 630 and 847 cover the suburbs where much of the fan base lives.
designCues.use: Side and suburb editions that sell where people live, from the south suburbs (708) to the North Shore (847).

designCues.cue: Water Tower limestone: the pale yellow-cream of the Joliet limestone Water Tower, one of the few buildings to survive the 1871 fire.
designCues.source: The 1869 Chicago Water Tower on Michigan Avenue, the city's symbol of survival and rebuilding.
designCues.use: A heritage base or tonal ground for 'I Will' pieces, under Bulls red and black.

designCues.cue: Lake-in-January gray: the cold steel blue-gray of Lake Michigan under a winter sky.
designCues.source: The view along the lakefront and Lake Shore Drive from December through February.
designCues.use: A base color for Hawk-season outerwear and fleece, set against Bulls red trims.

designCues.cue: Mild sauce red-orange: the sweet, tangy sauce on wings and fish at South and West Side chicken and fish shacks.
designCues.source: Black-owned neighborhood spots such as Harold's Chicken Shack and countless wing joints.
designCues.use: A secondary accent for a food-culture capsule, made only in partnership with named local businesses that are credited and paid.

designCues.cue: The Hawk-season stadium parka: knee-length, wind-blocking, with a hood cut to fit over a fitted cap, storm cuffs and reflective piping.
designCues.source: Fans walking from the L or the Madison bus to the United Center in January.
designCues.use: The hero Chicago game-day piece, in Bulls black with lake-gray lining and red reflective details.

productHooks: 'Madison Street' collection: split North/South hoodies and tees carrying the 0/0 grid coordinate and 1901 W. Madison, sold at the United Center and at shops on all sides of the city as a one-city statement.
'Hawk Season' outerwear drop before the first freeze in November: stadium parka, heavyweight fleece and a cuffed knit hat with a hidden Y-device patch, built for the walk from the bus or L.
A Chicago-first 'Gym Shoes' basketball footwear pack and campaign that uses the local word, launched through Public League and park-league programs rather than downtown retail alone.
'I Will' shooting shirts and tees for the young Splitter-era core (Giddey, Buzelis, Caleb Wilson), with Sandburg lines printed inside, released around Chicago's 190th birthday on March 4, 2027.

Neighborhood editions for the 77 community areas, co-designed and paid with local creatives in places such as Bronzeville, Little Village, Humboldt Park and Chatham, with bilingual tags where it fits.
A Bud Billiken back-to-school kids' collection (August 2027) made with Chicago Defender Charities, pairing Benny the Bull gear with gym shoes and giving back to South Side schools.
watchouts: Never use 'Chiraq', crime-tape or bullet imagery, or drill-scene and gang-linked slang. These tie to real deaths, and Chicagoans resent being used as a national crime talking point.

Latino neighborhoods have lived under federal immigration enforcement since fall 2025. Activations there must be community-led and bilingual, must not collect data or film residents, and must not borrow protest symbols such as whistles.

Chicago is Council of Three Fires (Potawatomi, Odawa, Ojibwe) homeland, and the name comes from a Native word for wild onion. The Blackhawks, who share the United Center, carry a long logo controversy, so keep all Native imagery off Bulls product and consult the American Indian Center for anything Native-related.

License or clear third-party IP: City of Chicago symbols (flag, seal, Y device), Bud Billiken and Chicago Defender marks, restaurant names (Harold's, Al's, Superdawg), FX's 'The Bear', and Cubs, Sox and Bears marks, which cannot appear on Bulls product. Jordan's name and likeness go through Jordan Brand.

Stay out of politics and ownership fights: Chicago holds municipal elections in February-April 2027, fans are frustrated with the Reinsdorf era, Chicago-born Pope Leo XIV is a point of pride that should never be commercialized, and figures like Kanye West and R. Kelly are off-limits.
